name: Rawdon, Quebec
note: Fishing locations for this city. Downloaded with the city's map, not bundled with the app. Every record here is marked unverified: the water, the species, the months and the hazards are researched, and the access scores and depth profiles are deliberately absent because inventing those is what gets somebody stuck in mud with nowhere to park. Every coordinate in this pack has been measured against the OpenStreetMap water geometry that ships in this region's own map file, so the pins are on the water they name. Zone 8 sets its periods and limits per waterbody rather than per zone, so the months given here are when the fish are catchable, NOT a statement that the water is open — look the water up by name in the zone 8 tool before you go.

spots.name: Lac Rawdon
spots.blurb: The lake the town sits on and the closest water to most of Rawdon. Two kilometres across, developed shoreline with cottages and docks most of the way round, a weedy shallow end and a deeper basin. A mixed warmwater lake rather than a trout lake — bass around the docks and the pads, perchaude everywhere, brochet on the weed edges.
spots.hazards: Almost the whole shoreline is private cottage land. Public access is limited to the municipal points, and walking somebody's lawn to reach the water is trespass whatever the map shows. Busy with boats and swimmers through July and August — fish it early or late.
spots.tip: The dock line is the fishery. Cast at the posts and the shade under the decks rather than at open water, and do it in the first and last hour of the day when the boat traffic has gone.

spots.name: Rivière Ouareau in the village
spots.blurb: The river runs straight through Rawdon, and this is the walkable reach: riffles, pools and rock within a few minutes of the middle of town. Smaller and more readable than the gorge downstream, and the most convenient piece of moving water in the district — the place to fish for an hour after work rather than plan a day around.
spots.hazards: Banks alternate between public frontage and private land, so read the signs rather than the map. The river comes up fast and dirty after rain and in the spring melt, and the rock is slippery wherever the water has been over it.
spots.tip: Read it as a small river: cast upstream into the head of each run, let it come back naturally, and work downstream. A light spinner or a tube jig covers it.

spots.name: Rivière Rouge at the confluence
spots.water: Rivière Rouge — tributary of the Ouareau
spots.blurb: A small tributary joining the Ouareau in the village. Genuinely small water — a stream you can cast across — and colder than the main river where it comes in, which is why it is worth knowing in high summer when everything else has gone flat and warm.
spots.hazards: Overgrown, undercut and narrow. Farm and road runoff after heavy rain. Low enough by late summer that wading it does more harm than good — fish it from the bank.
spots.tip: The confluence itself is the spot: cold water meeting warm, and fish sitting in the seam. Small bait, light line, and approach from downstream where they cannot see you.

spots.name: Lac Scaby
spots.blurb: A small lake on the south side of the village, a couple of hundred metres across. Shallow, weedy and warm — which makes it poor trout water and good panfish water. The kind of place to take somebody who has not fished before, because something will bite.
spots.hazards: Small and ringed with private frontage, so access is limited and worth checking before you walk down. Weeds up badly from July. Soft margins.
spots.tip: A small piece of worm under a float a metre down, next to any weed. Nothing else is needed and nothing else works better.

spots.name: Lac Pontbriand
spots.blurb: A quieter lake just west of the village with less development than Lac Rawdon and colder water at the deep end. Panfish and brochet along the margins, and enough depth that brook trout hold through the summer where the springs come in.
spots.hazards: Shoreline cottages again, and the launch is small. The shallow end weeds up badly by August. Cold water well into May — this lake warms later than it looks like it should.
spots.tip: Work the inflow in spring and autumn. That is where the cold water arrives and it is the only part of this lake worth a brook trout cast.

spots.name: Parc Régional des Chutes Dorwin
spots.blurb: The waterfall park on the Ouareau, and the best-known piece of water in Rawdon for reasons that have nothing to do with fishing. Below the falls the river runs through a rocky gorge into a series of pools — cold, clean, boulder-strewn water that holds smallmouth in the pools and brook trout in the cold seams.
spots.hazards: A GORGE WITH A WATERFALL IN IT. The rock is slick with spray and moss year-round, the drop from the viewing areas is lethal, and people have died here. Stay on the marked trails and out of the water at the falls themselves. The park charges admission and has opening hours — this is not dawn-to-dark access.
spots.tip: Fish the pools well below the falls, not the plunge pool. Cast upstream into the head of a pool and let a tube jig come back with the current over the boulders.

spots.name: Parc des Cascades
spots.blurb: The other Ouareau park, upstream and west of town: a long run of rapids and rock shelves with flatter water between them. Busier with swimmers than with anglers through July and August, which is the trade — easy parking and a made path, in exchange for company.
spots.hazards: Fast water over smooth rock, and the shelves are slippery well above the waterline. Swimming crowds in summer mean you are casting around people — go early. Levels move quickly after rain.
spots.tip: Fish the slack behind the shelves rather than the white water. A smallmouth sitting out of the current will take a tube dropped just off the edge of the flow.

spots.name: Lac Kildare
spots.blurb: A small lake in the old Kildare township east of Rawdon, about half a kilometre across. Quiet, shallow around the edges, with a modest deeper middle. A panfish and bass lake rather than anything more ambitious, and close enough to be an evening rather than an outing.
spots.hazards: Cottage frontage and limited public access — check before you walk in. Shallow margins weed up through the summer and the bottom is soft in the bays.
spots.tip: Work the edge where the weed stops and the bottom drops. A small spinner along that line will find the bass and the perchaude both.

spots.name: Rivière Blanche
spots.blurb: A small river running east of Rawdon through farmland and bush, smaller than the Ouareau and much less fished. Rocky runs and undercut banks, with enough shade that it stays cool into the summer. Worth knowing precisely because almost nobody bothers with it.
spots.hazards: Mostly farmland frontage, so access is the road crossings and nothing else — walking a field to the water is trespass. Brush, undercut banks, and agricultural runoff after heavy rain.
spots.tip: Work upstream, cast into the head of each run, and keep out of sight. Small water means the fish see you before you see them.

spots.name: Lac Maskinongé
spots.blurb: A large, relatively shallow and fertile lake well east of Rawdon, and the walleye water of the district — doré jaune is what people come here for. Named for the maskinongé, which are still in it and still very hard to catch. This is the drive-out lake rather than the after-work one, and the drive is the price of the doré.
spots.hazards: Shallow and large, which is the combination that builds a short steep chop fast — this lake gets dangerous in a wind quicker than its size suggests. Weed growth is heavy from July. A summer town with a busy launch.
spots.tip: Doré water, and doré here means low light. Fish the last hour of the evening on the break where a flat drops into the basin, and measure everything: 37 to 53 cm goes back and that is most of what you will catch.

spots.name: Rivière L'Assomption
spots.blurb: The main river of Lanaudière, wider and slower than the Ouareau, with deep pools, current breaks and a mixed river fishery — doré and dorés noirs in the pools, smallmouth on the rock, and the occasional maskinongé that will ruin your tackle. Worth the drive when the small water at home has gone low and clear.
spots.hazards: Steep banks in places and a current stronger than the surface suggests after rain. Spring levels come up fast with the melt. Long stretches are private frontage; the public access is at the bridges and the town parks.
spots.tip: Fish the pools and the seams behind the current breaks, not the open flow. Cast upstream and let the bait come back naturally with the water.

spots.name: Lac Ouareau
spots.blurb: The big deep lake of the district, up in the Laurentians. Genuinely cold and deep enough to hold touladi through the summer, which none of the lakes nearer Rawdon can do. Also brochet in the bays and perchaude everywhere. A proper day out rather than an evening.
spots.hazards: Big water that builds a real chop when the wind comes down the length of it, and the shoreline is mostly rock with few places to get out. Cold enough year-round that going in is a serious matter. Boat access dominates; shore fishing is limited to the public points.
spots.tip: The touladi are a shore fish for two or three weeks after ice-out and then they are gone deep until autumn. If you are here in July, fish the bays for brochet instead and come back in May.
